items.title: Epsilon-NFAs, finite epsilon closure, and extended word transition
items.statement: An epsilon-NFA is N=(Q,Sigma,delta,q0,F), with finite Q, q0 in Q, F subset Q, finite alphabet Sigma and total delta:Q x (Sigma disjoint-union {epsilon}) -> P(Q); missing diagram arrows mean empty transition sets. Epsilon is a tagged empty-input label, not a letter. For S subset Q put C0=S and C(k+1)=Ck union union_{q in Ck}delta(q,epsilon). ECl(S)=C|Q| is the least epsilon-closed superset of S; ECl(q) abbreviates ECl({q}). Define widehat-delta:P(Q) x Sigma* -> P(Q) by widehat-delta(S,epsilon)=ECl(S) and widehat-delta(S,ua)=ECl(union_{q in widehat-delta(S,u)}delta(q,a)); widehat-delta(q,w)=widehat-delta({q},w). These are exactly endpoints of finite paths spelling w after erasing epsilon labels. Acceptance means widehat-delta(q0,w) intersects F, defining L(N).
items.strategy: Package the well-definedness arguments here, before the theorem uses the interface. thm-recursion on P(Q) builds Ck. It is increasing; every strict inclusion increases finite cardinality by thm-subset-of-a-finite-set, so Cn=C(n+1) for n=|Q| (otherwise n+1 strict increases force cardinality >n). Equality persists; induction proves containment in each closed superset. Ck consists exactly of endpoints of epsilon paths of at most k edges, proved in both directions by deleting/appending the last edge. Thus ECl is extensive, monotone, idempotent, preserves unions, and ECl(empty)=empty; no graph or fixed-point theorem is imported. For a fixed word of length r, thm-recursion on N x P(Q), with index carried in the value and a frozen update after r, gives its unique sequence of state sets. Prove uniqueness and compatibility on prefixes by induction; Separation in the available function set packages all words. A finite path spelling ua splits at its last letter edge into a path spelling u, that edge, and an epsilon suffix; this gives both inclusions in the endpoint interpretation. All assertions are finite-set arguments in ZF. No later NFA item is cited.

references.title: Jean Gallier, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (2018), §§3.3–3.5
Alfred Aho, COMS W3261 Lecture 3, §§1–2

items.title: Subset construction and its exact reachability invariant
items.statement: For every epsilon-NFA N, D_N=(P(Q),Sigma,mu,S0,G) is a total DFA, where S0=ECl({q0}), mu(S,a)=ECl(union_{q in S}delta(q,a)), and G={S subset Q:S intersects F}. For every S subset Q and w in Sigma*, mu*(ECl(S),w)=widehat-delta(S,w); in particular mu*(S0,w)=widehat-delta(q0,w), hence L(D_N)=L(N). The state set has 2^|Q| elements, and empty is a legitimate absorbing state.
items.strategy: First use finite power-set cardinality to establish a finite, nonempty DFA state set; every transition lands in P(Q), including at empty. The earlier DFA existence theorem supplies mu*. Induct on word length for the displayed invariant: base is ECl(S), and the successor step substitutes the induction hypothesis into mu. The final-state test then gives language equality in both directions. Do not assert mu*(S,w)=widehat-delta(S,w) for unclosed S: it already fails at epsilon. Gallier restricts to closed subsets, while the present full-power-set convention matches the legacy supplier and Aho. An optional reachable-state table is an example, not a different theorem or a minimization assertion.

references.title: Jean Gallier, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (2018), §§3.3–3.5
Alfred Aho, COMS W3261 Lecture 3, §§1–2

items.title: A DFA embeds as an epsilon-free NFA
items.statement: For a total DFA D=(Q,Sigma,d,q0,F), let N_D have the same Q,Sigma,q0,F, delta(q,a)={d(q,a)} and delta(q,epsilon)=empty. Then widehat-delta_N_D(q,w)={d*(q,w)} for every q,w and L(N_D)=L(D).
items.strategy: Check the NFA tuple, prove ECl(S)=S because epsilon transitions are empty, and induct on word length for the singleton identity. Acceptance follows by intersecting the singleton with F. The direction is DFA to NFA; no subset theorem or later equivalence corollary is a premise.

references.title: Jean Gallier, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (2018), §§3.3–3.5
Alfred Aho, COMS W3261 Lecture 3, §§1–2

title: Finite-Automata Transition and Determinisation Interfaces: Examples

items.title: Epsilon closure and word transitions on three states
items.statement: Let Q={p,q,r}, Sigma={a,b}, q0=p, F={r}; delta(p,epsilon)={q}, delta(q,a)={q,r}, delta(r,b)={r}, and all other entries are empty. Then ECl({p})={p,q}, ECl(empty)=empty; from p the state sets after epsilon,a,aa,ab,b,aba are respectively {p,q},{q,r},{q,r},{r},empty,empty. Thus a,aa,ab are accepted and epsilon,b,aba are rejected.
items.strategy: Write all nine entries (three labels at three states); compute every closure and each listed word using the recursion. The example uses a local three-state witness rather than importing Gallier’s four-state suffix automaton.

references.title: Jean Gallier, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (2018), §§3.3–3.5
Alfred Aho, COMS W3261 Lecture 3, §§1–2

items.title: A complete determinisation table for a three-state epsilon-NFA
items.statement: For Q={p,q,r}, Sigma={a,b}, start p, final set {r}, delta(p,epsilon)={q}, delta(q,a)={q,r}, delta(r,b)={r}, and all other entries empty, the reachable subset states are A={p,q}, B={q,r}, C={r}, Z=empty. Their (a,b) rows are A:(B,Z), B:(B,C), C:(Z,C), Z:(Z,Z); start A, final states B,C. The other four of the eight full-power-set states are unreachable.
items.strategy: Restate the whole NFA instead of depending on the generated companion example. Calculate each table entry; A,B,C,Z are reached by epsilon,a,ab,b. Closure of these four under each letter, with the theorem, proves exhaustiveness for all words; no finite smoke test substitutes for this induction.

references.title: Jean Gallier, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (2018), §§3.3–3.5
Alfred Aho, COMS W3261 Lecture 3, §§1–2

items.title: Dropping epsilon closure changes the accepted language
items.statement: The claim that epsilon closure can be omitted from determinisation is false. Let Q={p,q}, Sigma={a}, start p, finals {q}, delta(p,epsilon)={q}, delta(q,a)={p}, all other entries empty. A construction starting at {p} instead of ECl({p}) wrongly rejects epsilon. Even with corrected start {p,q}, omitting post-letter closure reaches {p} on a and rejects, while the true state set is {p,q} and accepts.
items.strategy: Compute epsilon and a directly. Treat the two defective algorithms separately: the first omits start closure only and the second retains start closure but omits closure after each letter. The two-state witness proves both failures without any undecidability or minimization claim.

references.title: Jean Gallier, Introduction to the Theory of Computation (2018), §§3.3–3.5
Alfred Aho, COMS W3261 Lecture 3, §§1–2

items.title: Initial tapes and machine-relative halting configurations
items.statement: Fix finite sets Q,Sigma,Gamma, blank sqcup in Gamma, Sigma subset Gamma minus {sqcup}, pairwise distinct q0,qacc,qrej in Q, and a total function delta:(Q minus {qacc,qrej}) x Gamma -> Q x Gamma x {L,R}. These data form the raw tuple M=(Q,Sigma,Gamma,sqcup,q0,qacc,qrej,delta). A tape is t:N->Gamma with finite support {i:t(i)!=sqcup}; a configuration is (q,h,t) with q in Q and h in N. For w:m->Sigma let t_w(i)=w(i) if i<m and sqcup otherwise, and I_M(w)=(q0,0,t_w). Relative to M, C=(q,h,t) is accepting iff q=qacc, rejecting iff q=qrej, and halting iff either; otherwise it is nonhalting. The right-infinite tape boundary convention keeps a left-moving head at zero when h=0.
items.strategy: Construct tapes inside Gamma^N and configurations by products and Separation. Piecewise cases are disjoint and exhaustive; t_w has support exactly m because input letters are nonblank, so it is a tape, including m=0. Distinct designated states make the accepting/rejecting predicates disjoint and the initial configuration nonhalting. The tuple is specified directly, without citing the later machine, tape, or configuration definitions. This is a boundary interface, not a definition of runs, a simulation theorem, or a proof that all computations halt. Keep the initial head at cell 0, not on a prepended blank, and do not impose a permanent end marker. Watrous’s two-sided tape and preceding-blank initial head, and Savage’s abnormal left-boundary termination, are source variants rather than imported conventions.

references.title: John E. Savage, Models of Computation, §5.1
John Watrous, Introduction to the Theory of Computing, Lecture 12, §12.1
Michael Sipser, MIT 18.404J (2020), Lecture 5, slides 8–10

items.title: The empty-input initial configuration
items.statement: For the raw tuple with Q={s,A,R}, Sigma={a}, Gamma={a,sqcup}, start s, accept A, reject R, and delta(s,x)=(A,x,R) for each x in Gamma, I_M(epsilon)=(s,0,t_blank), where t_blank(i)=sqcup for all i. Its tape support is empty and it is nonhalting.
items.strategy: Specify all nonhalting transitions and evaluate the initial-tape formula at length zero. Head position zero persists as a valid coordinate even though the input has no letters; do not infer that the initial configuration is accepting from the empty input.

references.title: John E. Savage, Models of Computation, §5.1
John Watrous, Introduction to the Theory of Computing, Lecture 12, §12.1
Michael Sipser, MIT 18.404J (2020), Lecture 5, slides 8–10

items.title: The same triple can accept for one machine and reject for another
items.statement: Take Q={s,A,R}, Sigma={a}, Gamma={a,sqcup}, start s and delta(s,x)=(A,x,R) for both tape symbols. Machine M designates A as accept and R as reject; machine N interchanges those designations. Both tuples have the same nonhalting domain. The triple (A,0,t_blank) is accepting for M and rejecting for N.
items.strategy: Check both tuples satisfy pairwise distinct states and totality on their identical nonhalting domain. Apply each machine-relative predicate to the same state/head/tape triple; the outcome changes without changing its tape or state component. No computation reachability is claimed.
